name: Song China
title: Social Hierarchy of Song China: From Emperor to Bondservants

tiers.name: The emperor
tiers.you: You are the Son of Heaven, who appoints every official and presides over the palace examination, but your ministers expect you to govern with them, and if you come to the throne as a child, an empress dowager rules for you.
tiers.kid: The Song emperor was called the Son of Heaven, and he chose the officials who ran the empire.
tiers.rise: The throne passed to a son or, when an emperor had none, to a kinsman: Gaozong, whose only son died young, adopted a distant descendant of Taizu, the future Emperor Xiaozong. Taizu himself had won the throne as a general.
tiers.why: The emperor (huangdi), the Son of Heaven (tianzi), was always a man of the Zhao family.

tiers.name: The imperial clan
tiers.you: You are a kinsman of the emperor, honoured with a title and kept on a state stipend, but barred from any post that carries real power.
tiers.kid: Relatives of the Song emperor were given titles and money, but they were kept out of important government jobs.
tiers.rise: Birth alone made a clan member. The distant kin cut off by Shenzong’s reforms had to make their way like other gentry, by study, office or land.
tiers.why: The descendants of the founder Taizu, of his brother and successor Taizong and of their younger brother Zhao Tingmei formed the imperial clan, the most honoured family in the empire after the emperor’s own.

tiers.name: Scholar-officials
tiers.you: You have passed the examinations after years of study and govern a county outside your home prefecture, in the robe of your grade; one wrong step in the quarrels at court could send you to the malarial south.
tiers.kid: Most Song officials got their jobs by passing very hard written exams.
tiers.rise: Most entered through the examinations: in the lists of 1148 and 1256 about 57 per cent of the graduates had no father, grandfather or great-grandfather in office, though most had other relatives in the bureaucracy. Demotion and exile awaited those on the losing side of a faction.
tiers.why: The scholar-officials (shidafu) governed the empire, and their households formed the privileged “official households” (guanhu), largely spared labour service.

tiers.name: Local gentry and landlords
tiers.you: You have studied the classics for years and sat the prefectural examination without winning office, but your family’s land and learning make you a leader of your county, whose cooperation the magistrate needs.
tiers.kid: Educated landowning families led their local areas, ran schools and helped the government officials.
tiers.rise: Families rose by buying land and educating their sons for the examinations. Property was divided equally among sons, so a family that produced no official for a few generations could sink back among ordinary landowners.
tiers.why: Below the officials stood a wider local elite: examination candidates, degree-holders still waiting for a post, retired officials and teachers, and the landowning families that supplied them.

tiers.name: Landowning farmers
tiers.you: You farm your own few acres with your family, pay the land tax in summer and autumn and sell a little silk or charcoal at the market; one bad harvest and a debt could make you a tenant.
tiers.kid: Most people in Song China were farmers, and in the warm south many grew two crops of rice a year.
tiers.rise: Study could carry a farmer’s son through the examinations into office. Debt, taxes and bad harvests pushed others into tenancy, and some indebted farmers fled their land to join the army.
tiers.why: Most Song people were farm families who owned some land, and in 1034 four households in five were rural.

tiers.name: Tenant farmers
tiers.you: You farm another man’s fields, hand over about half of your harvest as rent and borrow seed and food from your landlord at high interest.
tiers.kid: Many Song farmers rented their fields and paid part of their harvest to the landowner.
tiers.rise: A tenant who saved enough to buy a plot could be registered among the main households, while many small owners sank the other way into tenancy.
tiers.why: Tenants farmed land owned by others.

tiers.name: Artisans
tiers.you: You work at your trade in your own shop, deal with the state through your guild when it requisitions goods, and teach the craft to your sons, but you may not sit for the jinshi examination.
tiers.kid: Song craftspeople made fine porcelain, silk cloth and printed books.
tiers.rise: A skilled craftsman could prosper and pass his trade to his sons, but artisans themselves were barred from the jinshi examination, so high office was closed to them.
tiers.why: Artisans ranked third in the Confucian scheme, below farmers but above merchants: scholar-officials saw them as essential producers rather than parasites.

tiers.name: Merchants
tiers.you: You trade in a great city, belong to a guild that sets your prices and may own a share in a ship bound for India, but scholar-officials scorn you, and you may not sit for the jinshi examination.
tiers.kid: Song merchants sent great ships to faraway lands and used some of the world’s first paper money.
tiers.rise: Barred from the jinshi examination themselves, merchants turned their wealth into land and into marriages with official families: in 1137 a military official was denounced for marrying his sister to the great merchant Pu Yali.
tiers.why: Merchants came last of the four occupations, scorned by scholar-officials as parasites, yet trade grew as never before.

tiers.name: Soldiers
tiers.you: You enlisted for pay, perhaps to escape a debt, and bear a tattoo, as convicts do; civil officials command you and look down on you, and your pay is small.
tiers.kid: Song soldiers were paid professionals, but people did not respect them very much.
tiers.rise: For a man without education the army was the quickest road up. Di Qing, born to a poor family and tattooed on the face, rose to the Bureau of Military Affairs, and Yue Fei rose from the ranks to command the armies that fought the Jin.
tiers.why: The Song kept a huge standing army, about a million men at its height, and in the 1060s defence consumed some 83 per cent of the state’s cash income.

tiers.name: Bondservants and slaves
tiers.you: You serve a rich household as a bondservant, bought or hired for a term of years, and the law ranks you among the “mean people”, below every commoner.
tiers.kid: Enslaved people and bound servants had to work for rich families, but there were fewer slaves than in earlier times.
tiers.rise: A bondservant hired for a term went free when it ended, and a maid might become her master’s concubine; many slaves ran away to work for wages.
tiers.why: At the bottom stood the “mean people” (jianmin), whom the law, largely inherited from the Tang code, ranked below all commoners.
